title: List edge-coloring conjecture
formal: For every finite loopless multigraph G and every assignment L of finite sets of colors to its edges with |\(\mathrm{L}(e)|\ge \chi ' (G)\) for every edge e, does there exist a proper edge coloring c with \(c(e)\in \mathrm{L}(e)\) for every e? Equivalently, is \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)\) for every such G?
why: The conjecture asks whether local restrictions on available edge colors ever increase the number of choices each edge must receive beyond the optimum with a shared palette. It tests whether ordinary scheduling feasibility is robust to arbitrary per-job availability, across all finite loopless multigraphs.

progress.text: Galvin proves \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)=\Delta (G)\) for bipartite multigraphs; publisher abstract and Kahn’s discussion checked.

Kahn, Theorem 1.1, proves asymptotic equality of list and fractional chromatic indices for multigraphs; because the ordinary index lies between them, list and ordinary indices also have ratio tending to one.
Molloy’s seminar abstract announces the simple-graph bound \(\Delta +\Delta ^{2/5} \operatorname{poly}(\log  \Delta )\). This still allows an additive gap; only the abstract was checked.
Jafari’s version 1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, claims the conjectured exact values for \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}, p\) an odd prime. These partial claims do not cover all complete graphs or all multigraphs.

definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map \(\partial\) assigning to each edge \(e\in E a\) two-element subset \(\partial e\subseteq V\). Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer \(k\ge 0\) let \([k]=\{1,\ldots ,k\}\), with [0] empty; \(\chi ' (G)\), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map \(E\to [k]\). A list assignment is a function \(e\mapsto \mathrm{L}(e)\) where each \(\mathrm{L}(e)\) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is the least \(k\ge 0\) such that every assignment with |\(\mathrm{L}(e)|\ge k\) admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree \(\Delta\) counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.

context_blocks.text: Think of an edge as a job requiring its two endpoint resources at the same time, and a color as a time slot. Jobs sharing a resource must use different slots. Ordinary edge coloring offers every job the same collection of slots. List edge coloring lets each job have its own availability restrictions and asks for a compatible schedule.

For two edges sharing one endpoint, ordinary edge coloring needs two colors. Lists {red,blue} and {blue,green} still each have size two, although their union has size three; choosing red for the first edge and blue for the second is valid. The conjecture compares the number of choices available to each edge, not the total number of distinct color names used across all lists.

Identical lists are permitted, so \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is always at least \(\chi ' (G)\). The question is whether arbitrary overlaps among different lists can ever create an additional obstruction. An ordinary coloring alone does not answer this, since a color assigned to an edge may be absent from that edge’s list.

The reference quantity is the chromatic index, rather than just maximum degree. A triangle has maximum degree two but needs three edge colors. If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every \(\varepsilon >0\), all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\le (1+\varepsilon )\chi ' (G)\). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}\) whenever p is an odd prime; \(K_{r}\) denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are \(p- 2\) and \(2p- 1\). These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.

sentences: A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to edges that share an endpoint.
In list edge coloring, each edge must choose its color from its own finite set of allowed colors.
The conjecture asks whether giving every edge as many choices as the ordinary chromatic index always suffices, even with arbitrary list overlaps and parallel edges.
It holds for bipartite multigraphs, and a general asymptotic theorem leaves only a vanishing relative gap.
Exact equality for every finite loopless multigraph would show that local availability restrictions never impose an additional per-edge palette requirement.
